title: Developing a Departmental Approach to Worked Examples
author: Craig Barton
summary: In the second post of his departmental-support series, Craig Barton describes agreeing four shared principles for worked examples with a department whose practice was inconsistent. These are empty hands and eyes up during the I Do, checks for listening rather than understanding while modelling, I Do on the left with the We Do revealed on the right only afterwards, and assessing the first We Do on mini-whiteboards. The key distinction is that asking students to guess a step they have not been taught is a check for understanding, while asking them to repeat something just explained is a check for listening. He also introduces Step-by-Step board checks, where students show just one step at a time, and says why this reduces data overload and gives more chances of success. The account of the CPD session, rehearsal and teething problems the next day makes the piece a realistic model of implementation.
points: Copying down the model as the teacher explains diverts attention to the previous step, so students should have empty hands and eyes on the board during the I Do.
During modelling the teacher should check for listening, not understanding, because quizzing students on unseen material slows the lesson and mostly produces wrong answers.
Revealing the We Do only after the I Do, beside it, keeps attention on one question at a time and highlights similarities and differences.
Step-by-Step mini-whiteboard checks cut the data load, pinpoint where students struggle, and give them more moments of success than checking only a final answer.
The CPD included rehearsal of the new checks with a partner before using them with a class, and colleagues tried the plan with one class for one week.
quotes: I remain convinced that it is a bad idea to ask students to copy down the worked example as the teacher is modelling it. Students’ eyes are looking down at their books instead of toward the board, and their attention is always on the previous step they are copying instead of the current step the teacher is explaining.

The difference here is subtle, but important. Asking students what is a good first step to solve an equation is a check for understanding. Explaining to students that a good first step to solve an equation is to subtract 3x from both sides, and then asking a student what is a good first step to solve the equation is a check for listening.

Asking for a volunteer or Cold Calling one student to see what answer they got means we run the risk of assuming their answer is representative of the rest of the class, and misunderstandings are likely to remain hidden. As is often the case, the mini-whiteboard is a maths teacher’s best friend here.

Step-by-Step reduces the amount of information a teacher needs to take in on any mini-whiteboard check. If 30 students have completed several steps on their mini-whiteboards, that is simply too much data to analyse in the few seconds boards are in the air, so things are likely to get missed.

Step-by-Step shows the teacher exactly where in the process students are struggling, allowing them to intervene and respond accordingly. If we try to assess several steps all at once, we end up having to play detective and working back from potentially lots of different final answers to see where the problem lies.

Students have more opportunities to feel successful. This should not be underestimated. If we only assess the final answer of a multi-step process, then that is just one chance for students to feel successful.

Rehearsal, as ever, was key. Checks for listening were new, and it was important colleagues got a chance to practice this in front of one pair of friendly ears, rather than doing it for the first time in the lions’ den of a Year 9 class.
